activity: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
story:
Eli wanted his bedtime book. He looked at the shelf. There were so many books. Some were big. Some were small. He did not know which one was his.

Mom gave him a card from his drawer. It was his birthday card. It had marks on the front. "Those marks say Eli," said Mom. Eli traced the letters with his finger. E, L, I. Then he opened the card. He turned the pages one by one, front to back. The pictures went in order. The cat jumped first. Then the cat landed in a pot of flowers. Eli laughed.

He held the card next to a book on the shelf. One book had the same marks on a sticker. E, L, I. The letters sat in the same order. "That one is mine!" said Eli. He pulled it down slowly.

They sat on the bed. Eli opened the front cover first. He turned each page the same way as the card. On the last page was a photo of Eli as a tiny baby. "That is me!" said Eli. Mom smiled and kissed his head.

activity: celebrating a birthday with family and friends
story:
Eleanor was four today! There was a big cake on the table. Her friend Milo came in with a gift. It had a red wheel printed on the paper.

"Open mine!" said Milo. Eleanor tore the paper off. It was a pretend tool kit, with a strong little hammer inside. "Wow!" she said.

Then she saw more gifts. She ran to the next one. She ripped it open fast. It was a soft bunny from Grandma.

Mom tapped her chin. "Milo is still holding his empty bag," she said. Eleanor looked at Milo. Then she ran back to him.

"Thank you, Milo!" she said. "I love the hammer!" Milo smiled big. "You're welcome!" he said.

Eleanor hugged the tool kit to her chest. "Time for cake!" Dad called. Everyone ran to the table.

activity: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
story:
Leah held her doll tight. "Big cart!" she said. Mom picked the big cart, not the small basket. Leah loves the big cart.

They went fast on the moving floor. Then they walked slow by the milk. "Cold!" said Leah, touching the frozen door. "Careful," said Mom. "The frozen door is very cold." Leah saw hot bread, too. A baker with big gloves held the hot pan. Leah did not touch. She just smelled it. Yum.

At home, Leah ate a small cup of ice cream. Then she slept and slept. She woke up. It was dark! "Is it morning?" she whispered to her doll. Mom came in. "No, sweet girl. It is still night." Leah looked out. Dark sky, dark trees. "Day and night are opposites," said Mom. Leah yawned. She hugged her doll and closed her eyes. "Night, night, sun," she whispered.

story:
Miles sat at the art table. He wanted to paint a big green frog. But the paint cups sat in the far corner. The corner was dark and dim.

He picked a cup in the dark. "This one is green," he said. He painted. Then he moved his paper to the window. The sun came in. In the light, his frog was blue! Not green. Blue.

"I could not tell in the dark corner," said Miles.

"You could not tell," said his teacher, Miss Ana. "It is hard to tell what color things are in a very dark place."

Miles carried all the cups to the sunny window. Now he could see. Red. Blue. Yellow. Green. He picked green. He painted a new frog. It was green all over.

The class dog, Biscuit, barked once. Miles laughed. Biscuit put his nose right on the paper.

"Do not sniff my frog," said Miles. Biscuit wagged his tail.

Miles spun around in his chair, one time, two times. Then he stopped. "Whoa," he said. "That made me dizzy." He held the table till the room stood still.

He looked at his frog in the sun. Green. Green. Just right.

activity: searching for a lost favorite toy
story:
Xavier ran into the grocery store. His soft bunny was lost. "Bunny, where are you?" he called.

Xavier ran fast. He ran from the fruit to the bread. He ran to the milk. He ran to the lunch meat. "I don't see bunny!" he said.

Mom held his hand. "Let's slow down," she said. "Let's look at one place at a time. Then we won't miss any places."

They looked at the fruit. No bunny. They looked at the bread. No bunny. They looked at the milk. No bunny. They looked at the lunch meat. There was bunny! He sat by the cheese.

"Bunny!" said Xavier. He hugged his soft bunny tight. "You were hiding by the cheese. Silly bunny."

Bunny's ear flopped over, like a little wave hello.

story:
Julia stood in the kitchen on the gray mat. Baby Sam was napping. Julia wanted to play music for him.

She took a big pot and a small pot. She banged them fast. BANG, BANG, BANG! The noise was very loud.

Mama came in fast. "Shh," she said. "Sam is waking up." Mama held the pots. "Loud and quiet are opposites," she said. "Let's try quiet."

Julia tapped the small pot slow. Tap, tap. It was so quiet. Baby Sam stayed asleep. Julia tapped again. Quiet as a mouse.

Then Mama made tea. Julia stood back, far from the hot kettle. Mama gave her a cold cup of water instead. Julia drank it all up.

Baby Sam woke up with a small cry. Julia ran to him fast, with her little pot. She tapped it quiet and soft. Sam smiled at her.

Mama peeked in. "Your quiet song woke him happy," she said.

Julia tapped one more time. Tap.

story:

The teacher knelt down beside her. "Let's mix some," she said. She poured yellow paint into a cup. Then she added blue paint. Nova stirred it with her brush. The paint turned green! Nova laughed and painted her cow on high, high grass.

"You found it," said her friend Sam. "Thank you." Nova smiled. Maybe she would dream about a green cow tonight.

activity: to recognise the letters of the alphabet and the sound each letter makes
story:
Charles sat on the big rug at book club. Miss Amy held up letter cards. "This is A," she said. "A says ahh, like apple."

Charles clapped. "Ahh!" he said. "Like animal!"

The kids sang the alphabet song. Charles sang too. "A, B, C," he sang, "all the way to P." Then he stopped. "Done!" he said.

Miss Amy laughed. "Keep singing," she said. Charles sang on. "Q, R, S, T, U, V, W, X, Y, Z. Z!" He looked around with wide eyes. "Where did Z come from?"

"Z was hiding in the song," said his friend Mila. She scratched her itchy sweater. "Z tickled my ears!"

"Does Z end the song?" asked Charles.

"Yes," said Miss Amy. "A starts it, and Z ends it."

Charles stood up. He found the letter cards in the basket. He laid them out on the dry, dusty rug. "A comes first," he said. "Z goes last." He put A at one end and Z at the other. He counted them all, one by one. Then he gave Z a big hug.

"Z waits so long," said Charles. "Poor Z. Now Z can sit by me."

Mila giggled. "Can A sit by me?" she asked.

"A is all yours," said Charles. "Ahh!"

story:
Raphael sat in the big chair at the doctor's office. He was excited! "Today I get a checkup," he said. His mom held his hand. An old truck went by the window. Raphael saw it with his eyes. Beep, beep! He heard it with his ears.

The doctor came in. She had a little stick and a lemon slice. "Open wide," she said. Raphael opened his mouth. First she looked with her light. Then she said, "Take a tiny lick of this." Raphael thought it would taste sweet like orange juice. He licked the lemon. Wow! His face scrunched up. His tongue told him it was sour!

The doctor laughed. "Good tongue!" she said. She let Raphael touch the lemon skin. It felt bumpy. Then Raphael smelled the lemon. It smelled sharp and fresh. "My tongue can taste that a lemon is sour," said Raphael. The doctor gave him a sticker. Raphael put it on his shirt. "Next year, lemon again?" he asked.

activity: to clap along to the steady beat of a song and sing a nursery rhyme from memory
story:
Kai stood in the garage next to Dad. Dad turned on a song. "Let's clap," said Dad. They clapped. Clap, clap, clap. Kai clapped too fast. Clapclapclap! The song ran away from him. "Chase the beat," said Dad with a grin. "It will wait for you." Kai slowed down. Clap, clap, clap. Now his hands landed right on the song.

Then Dad sang, "The itsy bitsy spider." He made his fingers climb up, up, up his arm. Kai tried too. But his fingers went down, down, down. Dad laughed. "Silly spider! Spiders climb up the spout." Kai giggled so hard his tummy wiggled. The spider went the wrong way!

Kai tried again. His fingers went up, up, up, just like Dad's. The garage smelled like warm oil and old paper. A cricket in the corner went quiet, then chirped along.

Kai sang the whole song by himself. Not one word missing. Dad scooped him up in a big hug.

Kai held very still, like a frozen popsicle. Then he whispered, "One more time?" His fingers climbed up, up, up.

activity: spending a surprise snow day at home
story:
Amelia woke up and saw white. Snow had fallen in the night. "A snow day!" said Mama. "No school today." Amelia put on her boots and her red mittens. Then she ran outside to the backyard.

The snow was deep and pretty. Amelia made a big snowball. She patted it and patted it. She made tracks like a little train, chugga chugga, all across the yard. Her mittens got wet from the snow. Her boots got wet too.

"I want to play more," Amelia said. She tried to put her mittens back on. They were cold and drippy. "Yuck," said Amelia.

"Your mittens are soaked," said Mama. "Hang them up to dry." Amelia hung her wet mittens on the line. She put her wet boots by the door. They dripped little spots on the mat.

Amelia watched from the window. She drank warm milk. Slowly the mittens stopped dripping. Slowly the boots stopped dripping too.

At last they were dry. "Now I can play again!" said Amelia. She pulled on her dry red mittens. She ran back out to her big snowball.

activity: searching for a lost favorite toy
story:
Mateo climbed into the car. He buckled his seat belt. Then he looked for Bunny. Bunny was not in his bag.

"Oh no," said Mateo. "Bunny is lost!"

"Let's look," said Mom. She turned on the light in the car. Mateo peeked under the seat. It was dark under there. He could not see anything at all.

"I can't see!" said Mateo. "It's too dark!"

Mom reached into her bag. She took out a flashlight. She clicked it on. "Here," she said. "A flashlight helps you see into dark spots."

Mateo shined the flashlight under the seat. The light made the dark spot bright. And there was Bunny! Bunny was tucked next to a shoe and a clump of dog hair.

"Bunny!" Mateo shouted. He grabbed Bunny and hugged him tight. "The light showed me!"

Mom laughed. "You found him all alone under there."

They drove to the store. They would sell their old stroller there. Mateo held Bunny all the way. He shined the flashlight at his shoes too. Click, click. Dark, then light. Dark, then light.

"I see everything!" said Mateo. "Bunny, look at your soft ears!"

Mom smiled at the mirror. "Home soon," she said.

"Bunny, we found you," whispered Mateo. "The light found you."

activity: getting a first haircut at a salon
story:
Luke went to the mall with his dad. Luke was getting his first haircut. The salon had a big fish tank. Little blue fish swam past the glass.

A hairdresser named Mia put a low chair for Luke. She brought a soft cape. It felt smooth on his arms. Snip, snip went the scissors. Then Luke heard a bubble sound. Pop! He turned his head to see the fish. Mia stopped cutting. "Your hair moves when you move," she said.

Luke thought about that. Why did his hair move? Because his head was attached to his head! If he sat like a statue, his head would not move at all. Luke sat very still. He kept his eyes on his knees. Snip, snip. The cutting went fast and neat.

Soon Mia held up a mirror. Luke saw short, tidy hair. "Can we come back?" he asked. "Yes," said Dad. "Next time we will bring Grandma to watch." Luke waved to the fish on the way out.

activity: to hold a pencil correctly and write the letters of their own first name
story:
Ava sat at the big table at writing club. Her paper was white. Her pencil was yellow. She wanted to write AVA all by herself.

She pushed the pencil on the paper. A. V. A. But her lines came out fat and fuzzy. "Oh no," said Ava. "My letters look like fuzzy bees!"

"Let me see," said Miss Kim. "Your pencil tip is dull. A pencil needs sharpening when its tip gets dull, and a grown-up can help." Miss Kim turned the pencil in the sharpener. Whir, whir, whir. Ava watched from her seat.

Miss Kim handed the pencil back. The tip was pointy now. Ava pushed it on the paper again. A. V. A. The lines were thin and clear. "Look!" said Ava. "My letters are not fuzzy bees anymore. They are just Ava!"

"Read it to me," said Miss Kim. Ava pointed at each letter. "A. V. A. That is me!" Then she drew one little bee next to her name, just for fun.

activity: going to the dentist for the first time
story:
Harper held her mom's hand at the dentist's door. "First time today," said the lady at the desk. "One little girl, one big chair, one tiny tooth check."

Harper sat in the big chair. It went up and up. Then the dentist came in. His hands were blue! "Why are your hands blue?" Harper asked. The dentist wiggled his fingers. "These are my gloves," he said. "I wear gloves when I put my fingers or tools in your mouth."

He pulled one glove off. Under it, his hand was not blue at all. It looked just like Papa's hand. Then he put the glove back on. Snap! It was blue again. Harper counted as he snapped each glove. "One, two. One, two." He counted with her.

"Open wide like a little mouse," the dentist said. Harper opened her mouth. She was a small gray mouse, squeak, squeak. The dentist looked at her teeth with a tiny mirror. All clean and shiny.

"Can I try a glove?" Harper asked. The dentist gave her one. It was too big. It flopped like a sleepy sock. "I will wear mine next time," she said. The dentist laughed, and the big chair went slowly down.

story:
Levi ran to the shape table at school. A big red clock sat there. "Look, the clock is a circle!" said his friend Mia. Levi grinned. He wanted to find a circle too.

He held up a tiny button. "This can't be a circle," said Mia. "It is too small. The clock is big." Levi put the button on the table. Then he put it next to the clock. He turned the button around and around. It stayed round, all the way, just like the clock.

"It is a circle!" said Levi. "A tiny circle!" Mia clapped. Then they found more. A square block. A triangle cracker. A rectangle book. "Big or small, they stay the same shape," said Levi. Miss Ana smiled. Levi put the button in his pocket. "My new circle," he said. "I will show my mom!"

activity: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
story:
Elizabeth went to the park with Dad. A picnic table sat under a big tree. Dad set up a little grill for hot dogs. Elizabeth wanted to help cook.

"Can I touch the grill?" she asked.

"Not yet," said Dad. "It can be hot even when it does not look hot. Only grown-ups touch it."

Elizabeth looked at the grill. It looked cool and gray. Was it hot? She did not touch it. She waited like Dad said.

Dad held his hand above the grill. Then he put a hot dog on. It went sizzle, sizzle. "It is hot," said Dad. "See the smoke?"

Elizabeth saw the smoke rise up. The grill did not look hot, but it was! The hot dog got brown and warm.

Elizabeth stayed close to Dad. She picked up her gentle blue blanket and hugged it. She sat on the safe side of the table. Soon the hot dogs were done.

Dad put one on her plate. It was warm and yummy. "You were a big helper," said Dad. "You waited so well."

Elizabeth smiled. "Can we cook again next time?" she asked.

activity: to put on a coat and zip it up by themselves
story:
Thomas put on his red coat. The zipper would not go up. He pulled and pulled. It stayed down by his tummy.

"Let's walk to the store," said Mom. "It is cold outside." Thomas held his coat shut with his hand. The cold wind came in anyway.

At the grocery store, Thomas tried the zipper again. His fingers pushed it. It went up a tiny bit. Then it stopped. "Almost," said Mom. "Try one more time."

Thomas lined up the two sides. He pushed the little slider up. It moved. It moved some more. Then it stopped at the very top. His coat was zipped all the way. Thomas smiled a big smile.

On the way home, Mom let him try again by the door. It took two tries. Then he zipped it up all alone. "I did it!" said Thomas. Mom clapped her hands. Thomas patted his neat red coat and walked with his hands swinging free.

story:

Avery tugged her dad's sleeve. "Dad! Dad! Look!" she said. The shop lady was still talking about a phone on sale. Dad held up one finger. Avery puffed her cheeks and waited. The shop lady stopped talking. Then Dad said, "Yes, Avery?" Now it was her turn to talk.

"Can I have the yellow cup?" Avery asked. "Let's look at it together," said Dad. He reached the cup down from the shelf. "Is it sharp?" Avery asked. Dad felt the edge. "No, it is smooth," he said. "Good," said Avery.

At the till, a boy stood in front of them. He put his apples on the counter. Avery waited behind him. The boy paid and danced a little happy step out the door. Then it was Avery's turn. She put her cup on the counter. "Please and thank you," she said. The shop lady smiled and said, "You waited so nicely." Avery hugged the cup all the way home.

Ben peeked over her shoulder. "That word looks like the one on the box," he said. Aubrey pointed to it proudly. "That says cookies."

story:

story:
Nora woke up and looked out the window. "It is rainy today!" she said. Big drops tapped the glass. Tap, tap, tap. Nora wanted to jump in puddles. She put on her sneakers and ran outside. She stepped in a big puddle. Splash! Her socks got soggy. "Oh no," said Nora. "Wet socks, wet socks!"

Mama held up Nora's orange rain boots. "Try these," said Mama. Nora pushed her feet in. They went right on. She ran back outside. She stepped in the puddle again. Splash! She looked at her toes. "My feet are dry!" she laughed.

story:

Isaiah saw a net behind each player. He thought the ball had to fly over the net. "The ball goes over the top, right?" he asked.

activity: to name the five senses and say which body part is used for each
story:
Max was at Grandma's house. A big truck went by. It made a loud rumble. Max did not like the loud sound.

Max put his hands over his ears. The rumble got quiet. He let go. The rumble came back loud. He put his hands back. It got quiet again. "Grandma, my hands make it quiet!" he said.

Grandma smiled. "Your ears hear sounds," she said. Max touched his ears. "Ears hear," he said. Then he touched his eyes. "Eyes see Grandma!" He smelled cookies baking in the oven. "Nose smells cookies!" He touched the warm cookie Grandma handed him. "Hands feel it!" Then he took a bite. "Mouth tastes it!"

"Five senses," said Grandma. "You are so brave with the loud truck." Max looked out the window. "Can we hear the ocean, Grandma?" he asked. "The ocean is far away," Grandma said. "But I can pour water in your bath. You can listen there." Max clapped his hands over his ears and off again, fast, like a game. Then he heard a bird sing, small and sweet. "I missed that bird before," he said. "My ears caught it now."

activity: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
story:
Ivy held the little box with two hands. Inside was her new puppy. He was small and brown and his tail went wag, wag, wag. Ivy named him Bean.

Dad stopped at the pet shop on the way home. "Bean needs a tag," Dad said. The tag was a small circle, shiny like a coin. Ivy picked a blue one. The lady put letters on it. Ivy pointed at the numbers. "What are those?"

"That is our phone number," Dad said. He helped Ivy squeeze the tag onto Bean's collar. The tag went jingle, jingle when Bean walked.

At home, Ivy took Bean out to the sidewalk. It began to snow, soft and slow. Bean saw a big leaf. He ran after it! He ran down the street, far, far away. Ivy could not see him. She felt a tear on her hand.

A neighbor came by, holding Bean in her arms. "This little one got lost," she said. "But look. His tag has a phone number. I called it, and Dad said to bring him here."

Bean licked Ivy's cheek. Ivy hugged him tight. "Your tag brought you home," she whispered. Bean wagged his tail, and the snow fell on them both.

activity: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
story:
Arya went to the library with her mom. She wanted a monkey song book. But all the monkey books were gone from the shelf. "Oh no," said Arya.

Then she saw a toy box. It had five little toy monkeys on top. A boy named Sam was there. Sam sang, "Five little monkeys jumping on the bed!" Then one monkey fell off. Sam put it in the box. Now there were four. "Four little monkeys jumping on the bed!" One fell off again. Arya counted with him. Three. Then two. Then one. Then the last monkey fell off. "No more monkeys!" said Sam.

"Let me try," said Arya. She put the monkeys back on top. She sang, "Five little monkeys!" She took one off each time. Five, four, three, two, one. Mom laughed. "You sing like salty popcorn pops," she said, "pop, pop, pop!"

Arya hugged the last monkey. "You fell down, little one."

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
story:
Rosalie put on her red team shirt. Her team was playing soccer on the grass by the big pool. The sun made the light sparkle on the water. "Can we swim after?" she asked Mama. "After the game," said Mama.

The ball came to Rosalie. She looked at it. Where should it go? There was a net at the end of the field. She kicked the ball hard with her flat shoe. The ball rolled and rolled. It went right into the net!

"Goal!" everyone shouted. Rosalie clapped her hands. So that was the game! Kick the ball into the net, and you score. The other team kicked the ball toward the other net. It went in there too. Everyone cheered again.

Later, Rosalie jumped into the pool. The water was cool and splashy. "Did you like the game?" asked Mama. Rosalie kicked her feet in the water. "The ball goes in the net," she said, "and then everybody yells!"

activity: welcoming a new baby brother or sister into the family
story:
Ali was in the backyard with Dad. They were waiting for Mom to come home. Mom was bringing the new baby.

Ali had a toy truck. He pushed it fast on the grass. "Babies like trucks," said Ali. Dad smiled.

Then Mom came out. She held a small bundle. "This is your baby sister," she said. Ali was so happy. He patted the baby on her head. He patted hard, like he patted his toy truck. The baby began to cry.

Mom said, "Pat very gently." Ali looked at his hand. He made his hand soft. He touched the baby's fingers, so so soft. The baby stopped crying. She held his finger.

Ali sat very still. Dad sat close by on the bench. The sun was warm. The baby looked up at Ali. "I will be gentle every day," said Ali. The baby squeezed his finger one last time.

activity: getting a first haircut at a salon
story:
Anthony sat in the car. Mom was driving to the salon. "Your hair is getting long," she said. "Today we will cut it."

Anthony held his hair. "Will the scissors hurt?" he asked.

"We will see," said Mom. "Maybe you can tell me."

At the salon, Anthony sat in a big chair. The hairdresser picked up her scissors. Snip, snip. Anthony closed his eyes. Then he opened them. Nothing hurt at all. It felt like nothing happening, just little sounds near his ears.

"Does it hurt?" asked Mom.

"No!" said Anthony. "Cutting hair does not hurt!"

Curls of hair fell down. One landed on his hand. He looked at it. It was so small and curly. How funny that it came from his own head.

Back in the car, Anthony found one more curl on his shirt. "Look, Mom," he said. "A souvenir."

activity: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
story:
Riley sat in the vet's waiting room. The sky outside looked cloudy. She held a small box with holes in the top. Inside was her new puppy, Ben.

Riley had a chocolate cookie in her pocket. She wanted to give it to Ben. She pulled it out slowly.

The vet saw the cookie and shook her head. "Chocolate can make dogs very sick," she said. "Dogs are never given chocolate." She opened a jar and handed Riley a small dog treat. "Try this instead."

Riley held out the treat. Ben sniffed it. Then he gobbled it up. His tail wagged fast.

Riley put the cookie back in her pocket. She picked up a toy snake from a basket and waved it. Ben jumped and barked. Then he sorted his toys into a pile with his nose.

At home, Riley fed Ben his dinner. She waited while he ate, bit by bit. Then Ben climbed into her lap and fell asleep.

activity: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
story:
Elena went to the park with her dad. She wanted a cold drink. Her juice box sat in the big cooler. The cooler lid was open. The lid made a shadow on the grass. "Open and closed are opposites," said Dad. He shut the lid. Then he opened it again.

Elena peeked inside. The ice was small and white. The cooler was big and cold. The sun outside was hot. "Close it please," said Dad. "The ice melts when it stays open." Elena pushed the lid down. Click. It was closed.

Then she heard a fast bird. It flew over the big slide. A slow snail sat by the tree. Elena sat down to draw the snail in her new notebook. She waited and waited. The snail moved one tiny step. Dad handed her a cold juice box from the closed cooler. Elena took a big, slow sip. "Nice and cold," she said.

activity: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
story:
Jasmine ran to the playground with her teddy bear. Her friend Mia was already there. Mia had a small toy pot and a wooden spoon.

"Let's play house," said Mia. Jasmine clapped her hands. She wanted to be the parent. She would stir the pot and mix the soup.

But Mia wanted to be the parent too. "I want to stir," said Mia. They both held the spoon. The pot tipped over. Pebbles rolled out like little beans.

Then Jasmine had an idea. "You be the parent first," she said. "I will be the baby." Jasmine sat in the sandbox. She hugged her teddy bear. "Ba ba," she said, very small. Mia laughed and stirred the soup.

"Now we switch," said Jasmine. She stood up and took the spoon. Mia sat down and drank from a tiny cup. "Ba ba," said Mia. The friendly sun shone on their pretend soup. Jasmine gave the teddy bear a taste too. "More, please," said Mia, holding out her cup.

activity: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
story:
Declan wanted to brush his teeth all by himself. He stood at the sink on his little step. The sink had two taps. He touched the left tap with one finger. It felt warm, warm, warm. Then he touched the right tap. That one was cold. "So one tap is hot and one tap is cold," he thought. "Which tap makes warm water for my toothbrush?"

He turned the cold tap a tiny bit. Water came out. It splashed into the bowl. Then it went down the hole. Where did the water go? Declan leaned close to look.

Then he saw something. It was a little box on the wall. It had two small holes. "What lives in there?" he wondered. Maybe his toothbrush could fit. Maybe his finger could fit too.

Declan did not put his finger in. He did not put anything in. He walked out of the bathroom. He found his grandma in the hall.

"Grandma, there is a little hole box on the wall," he said. "I did not touch it."

Grandma held his hand. They went back together. "That is called an outlet," she said. "No fingers, no sticks, no toys in there. Ever."

"Never put things in the outlet," said Declan.

"That's right," said Grandma. She turned the warm water on for him. Declan brushed his teeth. The water was warm, just right. Then he saw a shy little spider peek from behind the cup.

"Hello, spider," said Declan. He waved with his toothbrush. The spider ran away.

activity: basic shape concepts such as circle, square, triangle and rectangle
story:
Emile was at daycare. It was snack time. He had a square napkin on the table. "Look, a square," said Emile. His napkin had four flat sides.

Emile had a wish. He wanted a little blanket for his toy bear. But the napkin was too big. So Emile folded the square napkin in half. He pressed the edge to the edge. He looked at it. The square was gone. Now it was a rectangle. "Teacher Nina, look!" he said. "My square is a rectangle now!" Teacher Nina smiled. "It is a nice long rectangle," she said.

Emile put the rectangle on his bear. It was just the right size. "It is not cold now," he said. Then his shoe tapped the floor, tap, tap. Emile folded his napkin again. He had an idea for tomorrow. He would fold it one more time and see.

activity: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
story:
Billie ran to the playground with Dad. The sun was hot on her head. The slide felt warm under her hand. Dad sat on a bench in the shade. "Stay where I can see you," he said. Billie waved. "I see you too!"

She went down the slide. She went up the ladder. Then she saw something far away. It was a red ball by the tall fence. She wanted that ball. She ran past the swings. She ran past the sandbox. The fence was far, far away.

Billie looked back at the bench. She could not see Dad. The tree was in the way. She could not see Dad at all. Billie stopped running. She stood very still. Then she ran back past the sandbox. She ran past the swings. There was the bench. There was Dad.

"I could not see you," Billie said. Dad held her hand. "Let's walk together," he said. They found the red ball by the fence. Dad picked it up. They took turns rolling it on the grass. Billie stayed close the whole time. "This is a good spot," she said. Dad smiled and rolled the ball back.

activity: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
story:
Matteo sat in his car seat. He looked out the window. "One big truck!" he said. The truck went beep, beep. Two dogs ran by a fence. Three birds sat on a wire. "Count with me, Mama!" said Matteo.

Mama laughed. "One, two, three, four," she sang. "Five, six, seven," sang Matteo. They passed eight red apples at a fruit stand. Then they saw nine balloons by a door. "Ten!" shouted Matteo. He held up all his fingers.

At the red light, a girl in the next car waved. Mama rolled down the window. "How old is he?" the girl's daddy asked. Matteo held up four fingers, just like the girl did. "I am four!" said Matteo. The girl held up her fingers too. "I am four!" she said. The light turned green. The two cars honked goodbye.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
story:
Eloise sat high up in the big stadium. Dad sat next to her. Mama and Grandpa sat close too. The crowd was loud. The field below was green and bright. Eloise could smell popcorn. It was her favorite smell.

The game began. Little people ran on the field. "Dad, they all look the same," Eloise said. She could not tell who was on which team. Dad pointed down. "Look at the shirts. This team wears red shirts. That team wears blue shirts." Eloise looked hard. One, two, three red shirts ran one way. One, two, three blue shirts ran the other way. "I can tell them apart now," she said.

Eloise counted the red shirts. Then she counted the blue shirts. A red shirt kicked the ball. The blue team got it back. The crowd stood up and cheered. Grandpa clapped his big hands. Eloise clapped her small hands. She waved her red scarf. "Go red team," she called. Dad laughed. The popcorn smell drifted up again. "One more," Eloise said, pointing at the field.
